newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Co-op battles to save mutual tradition.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Co-op battles to save mutual tradition.

text.p: A battle among London's top financiers over a British consumer services group could spell the end of a 150-year-old tradition of small businesses and individuals clubbing together for mutual gain.

The Manchester-based Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS), founded in 1863 to serve the needs of consumer co-operatives, now supplies most of Britain's co-operative retail societies with everything from babyfood to coffins.
But it is currently fighting off the multi-billion pound attentions of a Guernsey-based investment trust and its backers.

"If, for strategic reasons, at some time in the future a decision is taken to sell any business, then it will be sold to maximise its value to CWS and not to an asset-stripping middleman," CWS head Graham Melmoth said this week.

Supporters of the CWS, which has appointed SBC Warburg to defend it from 31-year-old entrepreneur Andrew Regan's Lanica Trust, say they want to defend ideals dating back to the "Rochdale Pioneers" of Lancashire in northwest England.

This group of artisans, regarded as the founding fathers of the worldwide co-operative movement, set up their first retail shop in Rochdale's Toad Lane in 1844. Co-op members now include actor Sean Connery and film director Lord Attenborough.
Their aim was to sell pure, untainted food to working people at a time when most food was heavily adulterated and was not weighed properly.

Their ideas spread as quickly as the Industrial Revolution itself and the co-operative movement is now represented in more than 100 countries around the world and has an estimated 700 million members.
The CWS has businesses ranging from supermarkets and funeral parlours to travel agents, an insurance company and the ethically and environmentally driven but profitable Co-operative Bank.

A Co-op insider said the international importance of the Rochdale Pioneers was reflected by the large numbers of foreign visitors, including many from the United States and Japan, to Toad Lane, now a museum.
The Pioneers were themselves inspired by social reformer Robert Owen who started an industrial career in Manchester in 1786, managing several mills and a wholesale business.

Owen developed what the CWS' Melmoth described in a history of the organisation as a "passionate concern about the consequences for working men and women of the Industrial Revolution" and formed his ideas on a new form of society.
The first Co-operative Congress, attended by Owen, was held in Manchester in 1831 and resolutions were put forward on the need for wholesale trading companies.

Early co-ops followed the principles of one man, one vote, a distributed surplus or dividend -- known as the "divi" -- on purchases, a fixed return on capital, protection for the consumer and a membership open to all.
It is the complex membership structure of the CWS, which employees 35,000 people and has a turnover of more than three billion pounds ($4.9 billion), that could now prove to be its saviour.

Regan is widely believed to want to offer its individual members around 1,000 pounds each but co-op shares are non-transferable and insiders say it would take a long time for such an offer to be made.

"He would find it very painstakingly slow. There would have to be changes on the boards at regional and local level because of the tiered structure. It would take him years and cost him a great deal of money," said one.

The CWS managed to secure a court order on Friday which effectively stymied Regan's ambitions, but his investment company Galileo said it was confident that its proposals would benefit members, employees, customers and the movement as a whole.
In an admission of temporary defeat, it said CWS members had been denied the opportunity to consider its plans "for the time being."
